finalGroupBindings.primaryGround: The Presidential Library page identifies the 1709 Poltava battle as the Russian victory over Sweden (L59) and calls it decisive, turning the Northern War in Russia’s favor (L68). The official chronology shows Narva, Lesnaya and Gangut are also real battles of that war but belong to 1700, 1708 and 1714 (L46,L48-L49), so all four choices remain one category and only Poltava matches 1709.
finalGroupBindings.locator: Poltava page L59,L68; Northern War chronology L46,L48-L49

finalGroupBindings.literal: Полтавская битва 1709 года стала решающей победой России над Швецией. После Полтавы стратегическая инициатива перешла к России.
finalGroupBindings.primaryGround: The explanation names Poltava and says the strategic initiative moved to Russia. The official history calls the victory decisive and says it led to a turning point in the Northern War in Russia’s favor.

finalGroupBindings.literal: В решающем бою под Нарвой 1700 года русские войска потерпели поражение.
finalGroupBindings.primaryGround: The note states that Russian forces lost at Narva in 1700, matching the Presidential Library account of the decisive November battle.

finalGroupBindings.literal: После поражения король Карл XII с небольшим отрядом бежал на территорию Османской империи.
finalGroupBindings.primaryGround: The note adds a concrete fact about the correct option: after the defeat, Charles XII fled with a small detachment to Ottoman territory. This is not stated in the prompt or answer label.

finalGroupBindings.literal: В 1708 году русские войска разбили у Лесной корпус шведского генерала А. Л. Левенгаупта.
finalGroupBindings.primaryGround: The note says Russian forces defeated Swedish general Lewenhaupt’s corps at Lesnaya in 1708, matching the Presidential Library chronology.

finalGroupBindings.literal: В 1714 году русский флот одержал первую победу над шведами в Гангутском сражении.
finalGroupBindings.primaryGround: The note states the 1714 date and that Gangut was the Russian fleet’s first victory over Sweden; both details are explicit in the retained Presidential Library Peter I context.
